transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky tells NPR his generals have told him the U.S. has
threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons access, but it has not happened
yet.
In an interview with NPR's Joanna Kekissis in Kiev, Zelensky says Ukraine will keep striking
Russia's war machine because he says Russian President Volodymyr Putin responds to force,
not diplomacy.
President Trump recently announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to a ceasefire in attacks
against energy infrastructure.
Zelensky tells NPR he found out about that announcement from Trump's truth social account,
not a phone call from the U.S. leader.
The Ukrainian leader also pushed back against Trump's accusation that Ukraine's military
actions against Russia are to blame for the record high cost of diesel.
He told NPR's Joanna Kekissis the blame rests with the war in Iran, referencing oil disruptions
over blockades in the Strait of Hormuz.
But Zelensky says that despite the often rocky relationship with President Trump, he still
views the U.S. as a reliable partner.
The United Nations says more than 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen from weeks
of fighting.
NPR's Eya Batrawi has the latest.
The U.N. World Health Organization says suspected cholera cases have tripled in the past three
weeks in Yemen, coinciding with the rising number of displaced people in overcrowded
camps.
Doctors Without Borders' mission head in Yemen, Ita Helend Hansen, tells NPR most people
being treated by the group have been women and children with diseases, malnutrition and
exhaustion.
People have had to walk very long distances in extremely hot weather, with burning sand
under their feet, limited access to water and food.
Being flared after Yemen's Houthis, who are backed by Iran, captured Western territory
from Yemeni government forces who are backed by Saudi Arabia.
Eya Batrawi, NPR News, Dubai.
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, has resigned.
NPR's Franco Ordonez reports the announcement of her impending departure was made this morning
by the new White House Press Secretary Katie Zechariah.
President Trump told reporters on Monday that he was not happy with Guilfoyle and that he
was considering firing her.
Zechariah broke the news that Guilfoyle was asked to step down during her first briefing
in front of the White House press corps.
We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign.
She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well.
Guilfoyle is a former top Trump campaign aide and former fiancé of Donald Trump Jr., the
president's son.
Wall Street Journal first reported last week that Guilfoyle had asked a donor to pay a
$100,000 credit card bill.
She allegedly asked him to wire the money to avoid a paper trail.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News, the White House.
From Washington, this is NPR News.
Cornell University says it is suspending parties and other social events at fraternity houses
for the remainder of the academic year.
The school is under investigation for its handling of reports of an alleged gang rape
in 2024.
Australia's government says it opposes the Pentagon's plan to livestream the December
execution of a former U.S. Army major.
He was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
Christina Kukliya reports from Melbourne.
Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says his government has sought advice on what
it can do to block the livestream of the Fort Hood shooter's execution by firing squad.
Speaking to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation, Albanese issued a warning to social media
platforms.
I'm making it very clear to them right now that as far as I'm concerned, this has no
place in our countries.
Australia's online safety regulator says it doesn't have the power to stop the livestream,
but would monitor if sites are complying with regulations requiring them to protect users
from harmful material.
This comes as parliamentarians across the Australian political divide call for the livestream
to be banned, echoing the bipartisan backlash in the U.S.
For NPR News, I'm Christina Kukliya in Melbourne.
U.S. home sales showed a modest pickup in September.
Here's NPR's Scott Horsley.
The National Association for Realtors says sales of existing homes rose by 1.5 percent
last month after a lackluster summer.
September sales were still down from a year ago.
High mortgage rates have been a drag on home sales, but that hasn't put much of a dent
in home prices.
The average sales price last month topped $417,000.
Scott Horsley reporting, it's NPR News.
